CausalChain: RMDN1 upregulation -> Formation of a context-specific repressive chromatin complex (HDAC1 + EZH2 + co-repressors) -> Inhibition of chromatin-activator recruitment -> Establishment of a repressive chromatin state (decreased accessibility & enhanced repressive marks) -> Downregulation of metastasis/angiogenesis-related oncogenes -> Reduction in tumor progression -> Improved prognosis in liver neoplasms
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in a molecularly defined subset of liver neoplasms, characterized by RMDN1 overexpression and specific tumor microenvironment markers, RMDN1 triggers a tumor-suppressive epigenetic mechanism by assembling a repressive complex that includes HDAC1, EZH2, and other co-repressors. Despite established evidence of HDAC1’s oncogenic activity in many liver cancers, we propose that under conditions of high RMDN1 expression, protein-protein interactions reconfigure HDAC1’s role, shifting it from promoting oncogenic gene expression to enforcing a repressive chromatin environment. This complex prevents the recruitment of chromatin-activating factors, thereby reducing chromatin accessibility and enhancing repressive histone modifications. The downstream effect is the silencing of key oncogenes involved in metastasis and angiogenesis, leading to attenuated tumor progression and improved clinical outcomes. Cutting-edge techniques—such as CRISPR-based functional screens, co-immunoprecipitation assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing—will be leveraged to validate this context-dependent switch and to precisely delineate the cellular heterogeneity underlying this mechanism.
Abstract: We propose that in a well‐defined subset of liver neoplasms—characterized by a distinct molecular profile including elevated RMDN1 expression—RMDN1 upregulation reprograms the epigenetic landscape by orchestrating a context-specific repressive complex. In this model, RMDN1 interacts with HDAC1, EZH2, and additional co-regulators to sterically and functionally block the recruitment of chromatin-activating factors. This event establishes a repressive chromatin state, as measured by decreased chromatin accessibility via ATAC-seq and increased deposition of repressive histone marks via ChIP-seq, leading to the selective downregulation of oncogenes that drive metastasis and angiogenesis. Importantly, this mechanism may redirect HDAC1’s canonical oncogenic function toward a tumor suppressor role. To validate this hypothesis, advanced methodologies including CRISPR-based screens, co-immunoprecipitation, and single-cell RNA sequencing will be employed to resolve tumor heterogeneity and reveal the mechanistic underpinnings governing the role-switch of HDAC1.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that RMDN1 upregulation would induce a repressive epigenetic state via association with HDAC1 and co-repressors, resulting in tumor suppression. However, it did not clearly define the subset of liver neoplasms nor sufficiently account for the established oncogenic roles of HDAC1 observed in clinical data. In the revised hypothesis, we explicitly delineate a molecularly defined subset of liver cancers with distinctive RMDN1 expression and tumor microenvironment features. We have incorporated additional mechanistic details to explain how RMDN1 may rewire HDAC1’s function from oncogenic to tumor suppressive by forming a complex with HDAC1, EZH2, and other co-repressors. Furthermore, we enhance practical implementability by integrating modern technological approaches such as CRISPR screens, co-immunoprecipitation, and single-cell RNA sequencing, thereby directly linking each step in the causal chain: from RMDN1 upregulation to formation of a repressive complex, inhibited activator recruitment, chromatin state modification, oncogene silencing, reduced tumor progression, and ultimately improved prognosis.
